narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 52% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped just above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. First, your LSAT score of 42 was the strongest influence, and it worked in your favor by pushing the prediction toward passing. Second, your third-year class ranking had an even larger negative effect. Placing in the 2nd decile is substantially weaker than the average 5.8 decile among accepted students, and this pulled the prediction strongly toward failure. Third, your undergraduate GPA of 2.4 also nudged the outcome toward failure; it sits well below the 3.23 average of students who were admitted.

In short, although your LSAT score helped, your lower class standing in law school and modest college grades outweighed that advantage and led the model to conclude you were more likely than not to fail the bar exam.

What you should do next is straightforward: focus on improving your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT if you can raise it further. Strengthening those two areas will have the biggest impact on future predictions and on your actual likelihood of passing the bar.
